parts.problem_md:
The equation of a curve is $y=(x--1)^{2}--6$

Write down the coordinates of the turning point.
parts.solution_md:
*Quadratic curves given in the form *$y=(x+a)^{2}+b$* have turning points at *$(-a,b)$

> *For *$y=(x-1)^{2}-6$* the value of *$a$* is -1 and the value of *$b$* is -6*

$a=-1,b=-6$

> *So the turning point is at *$( - ( - 1 ) , - 6 )$*.*

**(1, -6)** **[1]**

![q15-4ma1-2h-qp-jan20-paper2-igcse-maths](assets/003-q15-4ma1-2h-qp-jan20-paper2-igcse-maths.png)

Complete the table below with the letter of the graph that could represent each given equation.

Write your answers on the dotted lines.

| **Equation** | **Graph** |
|---|---|
| $y=\frac{2}{x^{2}}$ | .................... |
| $y=-\frac{1}{2}x^{3}$ | .................... |
| $y=-\frac{5}{x}$ | .................... |
parts.solution_md:
> *Consider each function separately*

- $y=\frac{2}{x^{2}}$* is a positive reciprocal graph with *$x^{2}$* on the denominator so it cannot have any negative **y **values - **C   *
- $y=-\frac{1}{2}x^{3}$*  is a negative cubic function which intercepts the **y **axis at the origin - **B*
- $y=-\frac{5}{x}$* is a negative reciprocal graph - **E   *

> *If you are unsure between **A **and **E  **for the last one, consider some coordinates and look at which quadrant they are in*

| **Equation** | **Graph** |
|---|---|
| $y=\frac{2}{x^{2}}$ | **Final answer:** **C** |
| $y=-\frac{1}{2}x^{3}$ | **Final answer:** **B** |
| $y=-\frac{5}{x}$ | **Final answer:** **E** |

**1 mark for each correct answer ****[3]**

parts.problem_md:
The curve $C$ has equation $y = ( x - 3 )^{2} - 5$

Using the axes below, sketch the curve $C$. 
On your sketch show clearly

(i) the exact coordinates of any points of intersection of $C$ with the coordinate axes,

(ii) the coordinates of the turning point.

![q21-paper1h-spec2016-edexcel-igcse-maths](assets/005-q21-paper1h-spec2016-edexcel-igcse-maths.png)
parts.solution_md:
> *This is a quadratic function so will be the shape of a parabola (∪)*

> *You need to find where the graph crosses the coordinate axes*

> *The graph crosses the **y**-axis when **x **= 0*

$x = 0 \Leftrightarrow y = ( 0 - 3 )^{2} - 5 = 9 - 5 = 4$

> *So the graph crosses the **y **axis at the point (0, 4)*

**[1]**

> *The graph crosses the **x**-axis when **y **= 0*

$y = 0 \Leftrightarrow 0 = ( x - 3 )^{2} - 5$

> *Add 5 to both sides*

$\begin{gathered} ( x - 3 )^{2} & = 5 \end{gathered}$

> *Square root both sides and then add 3 to both sides*

$\begin{gathered} x - 3 & = \pm \sqrt{5} \\ x = 3 \pm \sqrt{5} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *The graph goes through the **x **axis twice, at the points *$(3+\sqrt{5},0)$* and *$(3-\sqrt{5},0)$

> *The turning point of *$a ( x + b )^{2} + c$*is at the point *$(-b,c)$

$a = 1 , b = - 3 , c = - 5 \Leftrightarrow \text{Minimum} \text{point} : ( 3 , - 5 )$

**[1]**

> *Draw the parabola by drawing a symmetrical ∪ shape which goes through *$(0,4)$*, crosses through *$(3+\sqrt{5},0)$* and *$(3-\sqrt{5},0)$* and has a minimum point at *$(3,-5)$

![edexcel-igcse-graphs-of-functions-ma-h-q9-graph](assets/006-edexcel-igcse-graphs-of-functions-ma-h-q9-graph.png)

parts.problem_md:
The curve$C$has equation $y=4(x-1)^{2}-a$   where $a>4$

Using the axes below, sketch the curve $C$. 
On your sketch show clearly, in terms of $a$,

(i) the coordinates of any points of intersection of $C$ with the coordinate axes,

(ii) the coordinates of the turning point.

![q20ii-4ma1-1h-qp-jan20-paper1-igcse-maths](assets/007-q20ii-4ma1-1h-qp-jan20-paper1-igcse-maths.png)
parts.solution_md:
> *This is a quadratic function so will be the shape of a parabola (∪)*

> *You need to find where the graph crosses the coordinate axes*

> *The graph crosses the **y**-axis when **x **= 0*

$x = 0 \Leftrightarrow y = 4 ( 0 - 1 )^{2} - a = 4 - a$

> *We know that **a  **> 4, so the graph crosses the **y **axis **below **zero *

> *The graph crosses the **x**-axis when **y **= 0*

$y = 0 \Leftrightarrow 0 = 4 ( x - 1 )^{2} - a$

> *Add **a** to both sides and divide by 4*

$\begin{gathered} 4 ( x - 1 )^{2} & = a \\ ( x - 1 )^{2} & = \frac{a}{4} \end{gathered}$

> *Square root both sides and then add 1 to both sides*

$\begin{array}{ccc}x - 1 & = & \pm \sqrt{\frac{a}{4}} \\ x = & 1 \pm \sqrt{\frac{a}{4}}\end{array}$

> *We know that **a  **> 4, so both answers are possible and the graph goes through the **x **axis twice*

> *The turning point of *$a ( x + b )^{2} + c$*is at the point *$(-b,c)$

$a = 4 , b = - 1 , c = - a \Leftrightarrow \text{Minimum} \text{point} : ( 1 , - a )$

> *We know that **a  **> 4, so -**a **< -4 and the minimum point must be in the fourth quadrant*

> *Draw the parabola by drawing a symmetrical ∪ shape which goes through *$(0,4-a)$*, crosses through *$(1-\sqrt{\frac{a}{4}},0)$* and *$(1+\sqrt{\frac{a}{4}},0)$* and has a minimum point at *$(1,-a)$

> *Note that *$\sqrt{\frac{a}{4}}=\frac{\sqrt{a}}{\sqrt{4}}=\frac{\sqrt{a}}{2}$

The diagrams A, B, C, D, E and F are six graphs of different functions.

![cie-igcse-q21-graphs-diagrams](assets/011-cie-igcse-q21-graphs-diagrams.png)

Complete the table to identify the correct graph for each function. One has been done for you.

| Function | $y=x+1$ | $y=1-\frac{x}{3}$ | $y=2x^{2}$ | $y=-\frac{4}{x}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Diagram | E |   |   |   |
parts.solution_md:
> *Consider each function separately*

> $y=1-\frac{x}{3}$* is a straight line graph with a negative gradient and a **y **- intercept at (0, 1) - **A*

> $y=2x^{2}$*  is a positive quadratic function with its minimum point at the origin - **C*

> $y=-\frac{4}{x}$* is a negative reciprocal graph - **D*

> *If you are unsure between **D **and **F  **for the last one, consider some coordinates and look at which quadrant they are in*

| Function | $y=x+1$ | $y=1-\frac{x}{3}$ | $y=2x^{2}$ | $y=-\frac{4}{x}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Diagram | E | **Final answer:** **A** | **Final answer:** **C** | **Final answer:** **D** |

**1 mark for each correct answer ****[3]**

parts.problem_md:
On the diagram, sketch the graph of $y = ( x + 1 ) ( x - 3 )^{2}$.

Label the values where the graph meets the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis.

![cie-igcse-2020-oct-nov-p4-tz3-q7b](assets/014-cie-igcse-2020-oct-nov-p4-tz3-q7b.png)
parts.solution_md:
> *Find the points of intersection with the axis*

> *Find the **x- **intercepts by letting **y** equal zero*

$( x + 1 ) ( x - 3 )^{2} = 0$

> * Solve by letting each bracket equal zero*

$\begin{gathered} ( x + 1 ) & = 0 \\ x = - 1 \end{gathered}$*       **and        *$\begin{gathered} ( x - 3 )^{2} & = 0 \\ x = 3 \end{gathered}$

> *So the **x** intercepts are -1 and 3*

> *x** = 3 is a repeated root so the graph at coordinate (3, 0) touches the **x** axis but does not go through it*

> *The graph goes through the **x** axis at the coordinate (-1, 0)*

> *Find the **y- **intercept by letting **x** equal zero *

$\begin{gathered} ( 0 + 1 ) ( 0 - 3 )^{2} & = y \\ ( 1 ) ( - 3 )^{2} & = y \\ y = 9 \end{gathered}$

> *So the **y- **intercept must have the coordinate (0, 9)*

> *If the brackets were to be expanded, the first term would be positive **x*<sup>*3*</sup>*, so the graph is going in the positive direction*

> *Draw the graph, remembering to include the points where it crosses the axes*

![cie-igcse-2020-oct-nov-p4-tz3-q7bi-working](assets/015-cie-igcse-2020-oct-nov-p4-tz3-q7bi-working.png)
